lead: This unit builds the foundation for image processing and computer vision: how a scene becomes numbers, how those numbers are arranged as pixels, and how simple pixel operations behave. After it you can describe an imaging pipeline, explain sampling, quantization and resolution, use neighbor and distance rules, and convert between RGB and HSI.
about: The unit starts with the origins and application map of image processing and vision (1.1), then fixes the standard processing chain and its physical components (1.2). It explains how the human eye and brightness perception shape what we call an image (1.3), and how light, sensors and digitizers capture one (1.4). Image formation is separated into geometry and photometry (1.5), leading to sampling and quantization and the meaning of spatial and intensity resolution (1.6). Pixel neighborhoods, connectivity and distance measures (1.7) prepare for arithmetic, logical and geometric operations (1.8). The unit closes with RGB and HSI color models (1.9), the representation used by later enhancement, segmentation and recognition units.

chapters.idea: Image processing and computer vision grew from the same need: to make pictures measurable and then to make decisions from them.
chapters.depth: Cover a short origin story: newspaper picture transmission, medical and satellite imaging, industrial inspection. Define image processing (input and output are images) and computer vision (output is a description or decision). Map applications by domain: medical, remote sensing, document OCR, inspection, robotics, entertainment, security, cheque and QR scanning. Some syllabi call the field digital image processing and the decision side computer vision. Keep history to one short block; spend depth on application examples that motivate later chapters.

figure.title: From scene to decision
figure.aria: A five-block chain runs from scene to sensor to digital image to processing to a decision, showing where image processing and vision sit.

chapters.example: Question: A shop scans a 1200×800 pixel cheque image at 8 bits per pixel. It stores three copies and sends them over a link. Find the size of one uncompressed copy in bytes and the total for three copies. Answer: 1200×800 = 960000 pixels; 960000×8 bits = 7,680,000 bits = 960,000 bytes ≈ 0.96 MB; three copies = 2,880,000 bytes ≈ 2.88 MB.
chapters.trap: Calling every image task computer vision; if the output is an image (enhanced, compressed, restored), it is image processing; if the output is a label, count or action, it is vision.
chapters.leave: Details of the processing chain to 1.2; segmentation and recognition algorithms to Units 4 and 6.

chapters.idea: A digital image system is a chain of acquisition, processing, storage and display blocks, and the textbook steps are functions placed along that chain.
chapters.depth: Cover the two views: physical components (source, sensor, digitizer, processor, memory, display, communication) and functional steps (acquisition, preprocessing, enhancement, restoration, color processing, compression, segmentation, representation, recognition). Define each in one line and show where feedback occurs. Some syllabi call the functional list fundamental steps in DIP. Do not derive filters; only place them. Include compression before storage or transmission and representation before recognition.

figure.title: Functional chain
figure.aria: A top-to-bottom chain places acquisition, preprocessing, enhancement, restoration, color, compression, segmentation, representation and recognition in the usual functional order.

chapters.example: Question: An image system has a 2048×2048 pixel sensor, 12 bits per pixel, and a 4 GiB pen drive (often sold as 4 GB). Ignoring headers, how many raw frames fit, and where in the chain would compression sit? Answer: one frame = 2048×2048×12 bits = 50,331,648 bits = 6,291,456 bytes = 6 MiB. 4 GiB = 4096 MiB; 4096÷6 = 682.67, so 682 whole frames fit. Compression sits after enhancement/restoration and before storage or transmission.
chapters.trap: Putting compression before enhancement or calling segmentation a low-level preprocessing step; the order follows the purpose, and feedback arrows are allowed.
chapters.leave: Filter design and transforms to Unit 2; coding methods to Unit 3; segmentation and recognition algorithms to Units 4 and 6.

chapters.idea: The eye is an optical and neural sensor whose nonuniform brightness response sets limits on what a displayed digital image can show.
chapters.depth: Cover structure: cornea, aqueous humour, iris and pupil, lens, vitreous, retina, rods and cones, fovea, optic nerve and blind spot. Explain accommodation and pupil control briefly. Define brightness adaptation (dark and light adaptation), brightness discrimination and the Weber ratio ΔI/I approximately constant over a mid range; exact constants vary, so use a simple numeric illustration. Name contrast sensitivity and Mach bands, but keep short. Some syllabi call this elements of visual perception.

figure.title: Light path in the eye
figure.aria: Light passes through cornea and lens to the retina, then travels by optic nerve to the brain, showing the eye as an optical sensor.

chapters.example: Question: A display has background intensity I = 50 cd/m². A test patch is just noticeable when its intensity is 52 cd/m². Find ΔI and the approximate Weber fraction. If the background rises to 100 cd/m² at the same fraction, estimate the new just-noticeable ΔI. Answer: ΔI = 52−50 = 2 cd/m²; ΔI/I = 2/50 = 0.04. At I = 100, ΔI ≈ 0.04×100 = 4 cd/m².
chapters.trap: Mixing up pupil (aperture control) with lens (focus) and rods (low light, no color) with cones (color, detail); also forgetting that ΔI/I is a ratio, not a fixed ΔI.
chapters.leave: Color perception and color spaces to 1.9; display gamma and enhancement to Unit 2; optical image formation to 1.5.

chapters.idea: An image is acquired when energy from a scene is converted by a sensor into an electrical signal and then into numbers.
chapters.depth: Cover electromagnetic spectrum bands used in imaging (visible, X-ray, UV, IR, microwave, radio) without turning into a physics chapter. Explain illumination, reflection and absorption, and sensor response. Describe single-sensor scanning with a moving stage, line-sensor pushbroom, and array sensor; uniform and nonuniform sampling. Define pixel, bit depth, frame and digitizer/ADC. Some syllabi call this image sensing and acquisition. Keep sensor physics qualitative.

figure.title: Acquisition chain
figure.aria: A source illuminates a scene; a lens focuses light on a sensor, and an ADC turns the sensor signal into a digital image.

chapters.example: Question: A linear sensor has 4096 elements, each 12 bits. It scans a page 3000 lines at 400 lines per second. Find the raw image size in bytes and the scan time. Answer: pixels = 4096×3000 = 12,288,000; bits = ×12 = 147,456,000 bits; bytes = 18,432,000 bytes ≈ 17.58 MiB (18.43 MB decimal). Time = 3000/400 = 7.5 s.
chapters.trap: Confusing sensor elements with display pixels; a line-sensor scan builds a 2D image over time, while an array sensor captures a frame at one instant.
chapters.leave: Sampling and quantization details to 1.6; camera calibration and lens distortion to Unit 5; photometric BRDF to 1.5.

chapters.idea: Image formation has two separable models: geometry says where a scene point lands on the image, photometry says how bright that pixel becomes.
chapters.depth: Cover pinhole and perspective projection, the thin-lens equation 1/f = 1/u + 1/v where f is focal length, u object distance and v image distance; magnification, field of view, and depth of field qualitatively. Define world, camera and image coordinates at a basic level. Photometric part: radiance L, irradiance E, reflectance, shading, Lambertian model, BRDF named only. Only a few universities teach the radiometric and BRDF detail; keep it short. Some syllabi call the combined topic image formation.

figure.title: Geometry and photometry
figure.aria: Scene radiance is collected by a lens, becomes irradiance on the sensor, and is converted to a pixel value, separating photometry from geometry.

chapters.example: Question: A thin lens has f = 50 mm. An object is at u = 500 mm. Find image distance v and magnification m. If the object height is 20 mm, find image height. Answer: 1/v = 1/50 − 1/500 = (10−1)/500 = 9/500, so v ≈ 55.56 mm. m = −v/u = −55.56/500 ≈ −0.111; image height ≈ 0.111×20 = 2.22 mm, inverted.
chapters.trap: Using the pinhole projection formula as if it included focus; pinhole gives geometry and infinite depth of field, while a thin lens gives focus and blur outside the depth of field.
chapters.leave: Camera calibration, epipolar geometry and stereo to Unit 5; color formation to 1.9; restoration blur models to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Sampling fixes which points exist and quantization fixes how many brightness values each point may take.
chapters.depth: Cover 1D and 2D sampling, sampling interval, sampling rate, the Nyquist criterion, and aliasing examples such as moiré. Define quantization: uniform and nonuniform, with bit depth b giving 2^b levels. Define spatial resolution (pixels per unit length or total pixels) and intensity resolution (bits or gray levels). Explain the trade-off: more spatial resolution or more intensity resolution costs storage. Some syllabi call this sampling and quantization; spatial and intensity resolution.

figure.title: Sampling and 2-bit quantization
figure.aria: Four analog samples 0.1, 0.4, 0.7 and 0.9 are quantized to 2-bit codes 0, 1, 2 and 3.

chapters.example: Question: A 1D signal is sampled at t = 0, 1, 2, 3 s with values 0.1, 0.4, 0.7, 0.9. Quantize to 2 bits over [0,1] using rounding to levels 0, 1/3, 2/3, 1. Give the output levels and the mean squared quantization error. Answer: levels are 0, 1/3≈0.333, 2/3≈0.667, 1, so codes 0, 1, 2, 3. Errors: −0.1, 0.0667, 0.0333, −0.1; squares 0.01, 0.00444, 0.00111, 0.01; MSE = 0.02556/4 ≈ 0.00639.
chapters.trap: Saying higher bit depth raises spatial resolution; bit depth changes intensity levels, while sampling density changes spatial detail. Aliasing appears when the sampling rate is below twice the highest frequency.
chapters.leave: Histogram equalization and interpolation filters to Unit 2; compression effects to Unit 3; resampling for registration to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Pixels become a usable image only after we define which pixels are neighbors, when they are connected, and how far apart they are.
chapters.depth: Define coordinates (x,y) or (row, column), 4-neighborhood N4, diagonal neighborhood ND and 8-neighborhood N8. Define adjacency, connectivity (4-, 8- and m-connectivity), path, connected component, region and boundary. Distance measures: Euclidean De = √((x−x')² + (y−y')²), city-block D4 = |x−x'| + |y−y'|, and chessboard D8 = max(|x−x'|, |y−y'|). Mention that m-connectivity avoids ambiguous crossings. Some syllabi call this basic relationships between pixels.

figure.aria: A 3×3 pixel grid has a centre C connected to its four side neighbours by distance 1 and its four diagonal neighbours by distance √2; Q is the diagonal point.

chapters.example: Question: Pixels p = (1,1) and q = (2,2). Find D4, D8 and De. Are they 4-connected or 8-connected? Answer: Δx = 1, Δy = 1; D4 = |1|+|1| = 2; D8 = max(1,1) = 1; De = √(1²+1²) = √2 ≈ 1.414. They are 8-adjacent but not 4-adjacent.
chapters.trap: Using Euclidean distance in a grid adjacency test: adjacency depends on N4 or N8, not on straight-line length. Also D8 is max, not sum.
chapters.leave: Connected-component labeling and region segmentation to Unit 4; distance transforms and morphology to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Arithmetic, logical and geometric operations treat images as arrays and change values, bits or coordinates.
chapters.depth: Cover the array image model. Arithmetic: add, subtract, multiply and divide; clipping/saturation versus wraparound; averaging for noise; differencing. Logical: AND, OR, NOT and XOR on bit planes and masks. Geometric: translation, rotation, scaling, affine and projective named; forward versus inverse mapping; interpolation nearest and bilinear briefly. Some syllabi call this image arithmetic and logical operations plus geometric transformations. Keep interpolation formulas brief because Unit 2 handles resampling filters.

figure.aria: A tree groups image operations into arithmetic, logical and geometric families, each with four common examples.

chapters.example: Question: Let A = [[200, 50], [10, 240]] and B = [[100, 20], [250, 30]]. Compute (a) A+B with 8-bit saturation, (b) A AND B bitwise, and (c) A rotated 90° clockwise. Answer: A+B = [[255, 70], [255, 255]]; A AND B = [[64, 16], [10, 16]]; rotated A = [[10, 200], [240, 50]].
chapters.trap: Adding 8-bit images with wraparound: 200+100 becomes 44, not 255. Exams expect saturation or clipping unless modulo is stated. Geometric rotation must use inverse mapping to avoid holes.
chapters.leave: Convolution and filter kernels to Unit 2; morphology to Unit 4; registration and affine estimation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: RGB is a device-friendly additive cube; HSI separates hue, saturation and intensity so algorithms can use color independently of brightness.
chapters.depth: Cover additive RGB, 24-bit color, bit depth per channel, the color cube, and primary and secondary colors. Define hue, saturation and intensity. Give RGB to HSI formulas: I = (R+G+B)/3; S = 1 − 3 min(R,G,B)/(R+G+B); H = 60(G−B)/(max−min) when max = R, with analogous cases for max = G or B; H in degrees, S in [0,1]. Mention HSV/HSB difference in one line. Cover pseudo-color and full-color processing names; color segmentation is left to Unit 4. Some syllabi call this color models.

figure.title: RGB to HSI
figure.aria: RGB values go through max/min, then intensity, saturation and hue are computed and combined into HSI.

chapters.trap: Using HSV's V = max as HSI's I = average; they differ. Hue is an angle, so 350° and 10° are 20° apart through 0°, not 340°.
chapters.leave: Color enhancement and color filtering to Unit 2; color segmentation and recognition to Units 4 and 6; color constancy and calibration to Unit 5.
